After the Michaelmas wedding, Rhys will be sent from the abbey grounds but will remain nearby on the cliffs, watching the lights of the house where Elara is imprisoned, until his reckless plan to see her one final time.

Rhys's oath at the final parting—that if Elara ever needs him he will find a way to her—combined with his banishment and his inability to bear the distance, will drive his reckless night return to the estate through the secret passages in the months after the wedding (Chapter 8, The Last Desperate Act).

chapters.name: The Sacrifice
chapters.content:
Michaelmas came in gray and gold, the last of the year's warmth burning off the sea like a candle guttering in its own wax. Elara woke in her tower room to the sound of bells — bells she had not ordered rung — and lay a long moment watching the light move across the ceiling, rehearsing the shape of the day the way one rehearses a death: first the lace, then the silk, then the walk, then the word.

They dressed her in her mother's lace, and the seamstresses wept a little, and she let them. Martha — the kitchen girl whose whisper had begun it all — held the train and would not meet her eyes. They wound Elara's dark hair up and threaded it with pearls, Marlowe's pearls, the very string her father would have hidden in the mews loft, and she wore them at her throat like a collar and did not flinch when the clasp bit. Through it all she thought of the mews — the crooked door, the smell of old straw, the way his hands had moved over the falcon's wing as if the bird were made of glass. That life was already a story told about someone else. She did not look at her own face in the glass, because the woman there was a stranger she had agreed to become.

Her father came to her at the door of the great hall and looked at her for a long moment, and something moved behind his eyes — pride, or grief, or both — but he only said, "You look like your mother," and offered his arm.

The chapel was full. Half the county had come to watch the Ashworth girl be sold, and they rustled and murmured like dry leaves. Viscount Marlowe stood at the altar in black and silver, his face a marble tomb, patient as a receipt. The organ wheezed. The candles leaned in the draft.

And Elara walked.

She walked as she had been taught since she could walk — back straight, chin level, the whole length of the aisle — and the world went soft and distant at the edges, watercolors bleeding into one another. She did not feel her feet. She heard her father's voice like something under water, the vicar's drone, the rustle of silk as she turned.

Then, through the tall window at the side of the chapel, she saw him.

Rhys stood at the edge of the crowd — the servants and tenants gathered outside, kept from the door by the steward's arm — and he was looking at her through the glass. His face was white and set, and his eyes burned with a grief so absolute she felt it land in her chest like a stone dropped into a well. He had come. He should not have come, and he had come, and she loved him for it and hated it and almost broke.

The vicar said the words. Marlowe's voice answered, smooth and cold as polished glass. Then the words were hers, and she heard them leave her mouth as if they belonged to someone else — I do, I do, I will — and the ring went on, and it was done.

She did not look at the window again. She could not. But she felt him there, all through the signing and the blessing and the slow procession out into the gray gold light, until the steward's voice and the closing of a gate told her he was gone.

The feast was a long, loud ache. Marlowe kept his hand on her arm like a manacle, and her father drank and grew almost merry, and the county toasted the salvation of Thornfield. Somewhere a fiddle played. Elara smiled until her face ached, ate nothing, and watched the candles burn down.

When it was over, Marlowe told her father they would winter at Thornfield while his southern house was set in order — a small kindness, delivered like a coin to a beggar, and her father bowed and called it generous. Elara understood what it meant: she would not even be carried away. She would simply be moved, like furniture, from one room of the cage to another.

Her new chambers were the best in the house — her father's old rooms, stripped of his things, hung with silk. The bed was vast and cold. Marlowe came in and stood a moment in his shirtsleeves, and said, "You did well today," as one praises a horse that has gone cleanly over a fence, and then he lay down and was asleep in minutes, breathing evenly, a man untroubled by his own wedding.

Elara lay beside him in the dark, the pearls still at her throat, and wept. She wept without sound, the way she had learned to do everything now, tears running into her ears and the pillow, until her chest ached and the night was old. Through the window the sea ground on, patient as a debt.

On the cliffs, beyond the wall, Rhys stood where the steward had set him out at dusk, and watched the house. One window burned late — hers — and he watched it until it guttered and went dark, and still he stood, the wind cutting through his patched coat, the salt drying on his face. They had taken his cottage, his keys, his name's last freedom, and told him to walk south and never come back. He had not walked south. He had walked up, to the high places, to the only view he had left of her.

Far out over the water, against the first paling of the sky, a falcon turned — once, twice — and was gone into the light.

Rhys put his hand on the stone of the wall, spoke her name into the wind, and made of it a promise he had already sworn: if she ever needed him, he would find a way to her. Not tonight. Not soon. But the oath was alive in him, and the pain was only beginning.

The sacrifice was complete. The cage was shut. And somewhere in the dark house, in a cold bed beside a sleeping man, the only woman he had ever loved was weeping into her mother's lace.

set.name: Lord Ashworth
set.description: Gaunt, gray-bearded master of Thornfield Abbey, crushed by debts, victorious and satisfied. At the Michaelmas wedding he gave his daughter away in the chapel, saw her married to Viscount Marlowe before half the county, then drank and grew almost merry at the feast, toasting the salvation of Thornfield. Kept his oath on his dead wife's grave: Rhys was spared, given his life and a little coin and sent from the abbey grounds with orders to walk south and never return — Ashworth did not have him framed or hanged. He told Elara she looked like her mother before offering his arm. Accepted Marlowe's plan to winter at Thornfield while the southern house is set in order. Weary, aged, satisfied the estate is saved, and still blind to the depth of what he has broken.

set.name: Rhys
set.description: Brooding young groundskeeper of Thornfield Abbey, orphan raised by old Tom. At Michaelmas, though banished from the abbey grounds — his cottage taken, his keys taken, told to walk south and never return — he defied the order to leave and came to the wedding, standing at the edge of the crowd of servants and tenants kept from the chapel door by the steward's arm, watching Elara through the tall window, his face white and set, his eyes burning with grief. Saw the vows spoken and the ring put on her hand; was shut out by the steward's voice and the closing of a gate. That night, instead of walking south, he walked up to the high places on the cliffs beyond the wall, the wind cutting through his patched coat, the salt drying on his face, and watched her window burn late until it guttered and went dark. At the first paling of the sky he saw a falcon turn over the water. He spoke her name into the wind and renewed his oath that if she ever needs him he will find a way to her. Weeping, heartbroken, powerless, resolved that her life was the price worth paying, and still nearby though banished — the oath alive in him, the pain only beginning.

set.name: Viscount Marlowe
set.description: Wealthy, cold nobleman, now married to Elara at Michaelmas in the chapel at Thornfield Abbey. Stood at the altar in black and silver, his face a marble tomb, patient as a receipt; spoke the vows smooth and cold as polished glass; kept his hand on her arm through the feast like a manacle. Told Lord Ashworth they will winter at Thornfield while his southern house is set in order. That night, in their new chambers, he praised her ('You did well today,' as one praises a horse gone cleanly over a fence) and fell asleep in minutes, untroubled by his own wedding. Unaware of Elara's forced acceptance, her bond with Rhys, the crushed scandal, or the man watching the house from the cliffs.

set.name: The Falcon
set.description: Young female falcon rescued from a rabbit snare, healed over six days in the mews, flew free on the sixth morning and circles the cliffs; the living bond between Elara and Rhys, invoked in Rhys's oath in the cave ('on the falcon's freedom') and in his oath at the final parting in the mews. At the first paling of the sky after the Michaelmas wedding night, far out over the water, she turned once, twice, and was gone into the light — witnessed by Rhys on the cliffs, a sign that freedom endures though they are caged. Still free, still occasionally seen over the cliffs.

set.name: Lady Elara Ashworth (now Lady Marlowe)
set.description: Eighteen-year-old daughter of Lord Ashworth, now married to Viscount Marlowe at Michaelmas in the chapel at Thornfield Abbey, before half the county. Wore her mother's lace and Marlowe's midsummer pearls at her throat like a collar; through the chapel window during the ceremony she glimpsed Rhys standing at the edge of the crowd of servants and tenants, his eyes burning with grief, and nearly broke but did not look again. Spoke the vows (I do, I do, I will), wore the ring, endured the signing, blessing, and the long loud feast where her father drank and grew almost merry and the county toasted the salvation of Thornfield. Marlowe told her father they will winter at Thornfield while his southern house is set in order. She has been moved, like furniture, to her new chambers (her father's old rooms, stripped and hung with silk), where Marlowe praised her ('You did well today') and fell asleep untroubled. Lying awake in the dark in the vast cold bed, the pearls still at her throat, she wept without sound into her mother's lace until the night was old. Hollowed, dead calm, mask of frost firmly in place; believes she will die by inches; desperately in love with Rhys; resigned to survival as the only victory.

At Michaelmas, Elara married Viscount Marlowe in the chapel at Thornfield Abbey before half the county, wearing her mother's lace and Marlowe's pearls; the vows were spoken, the ring put on, the signing and blessing done, and the marriage was sealed.

During the ceremony Elara saw Rhys through the tall chapel window, standing at the edge of the crowd of servants and tenants outside, his face white and set, his eyes burning with grief; she nearly broke but did not look at the window again.

At the wedding feast Viscount Marlowe told Lord Ashworth they will winter at Thornfield while his southern house is set in order, so Elara will remain in the abbey, moved like furniture from one room of the cage to another.

Banished from the abbey grounds (cottage, keys, and name taken; told to walk south and never return), Rhys instead climbed to the high cliffs beyond the wall and watched Elara's window burn late into the wedding night until it guttered and went dark; at dawn he saw the falcon turn over the water and renewed his oath to find a way to her if she ever needs him.

In her cold new chambers on her wedding night, while Marlowe slept untroubled beside her, Elara lay awake with the pearls at her throat and wept without sound into her mother's lace until the night was old.

Months after the wedding, Rhys — unable to bear the distance and bound by his oath — will slip back into the estate through the abbey's secret passages under cover of darkness, hoping only for a glimpse of Elara, in Chapter 8 (The Last Desperate Act).

chapters.name: The Last Desperate Act
chapters.content:
The winter came down over Thornfield like a lid, and Elara learned to live under it.

Months passed. The Michaelmas gold rotted into November mud, the mud froze, and the sea turned iron under a pewter sky. She was Lady Marlowe now, and the name sat on her the way a stone sits in a pocket, carried everywhere, useful for nothing. She rose when the house rose, smiled when the county called, said my lord in the right places. Marlowe was not cruel; he was simply elsewhere, reading his ledgers at dinner, sleeping like a stone, touching her with the absent certainty of a man touching his own furniture. She had thought she would die of it by inches; instead she discovered one can survive anything, and that survival is its own slow wound.

Only the cliffs were left to her. From her window — her father's old window, the best in the house — she could see the headland where the storm had caught them, the hollow where the tide had hidden them, the long crumble of the path they had climbed hand in hand into a world washed new. And once, in a hard white January noon, she saw the falcon, a dark arrow against the snow-light, turning once over the water, and gone. She stood at the glass until her breath froze on it, and told herself the bird meant nothing.

She did not know where Rhys was. Her father's bargain had set him beyond the wall, and beyond the wall was a country she could not cross. The servants whispered of the man who lived in the sea cave at the foot of the headland, a wild thing, they said, who watched the abbey like a dog watches a shut door. She never asked; asking would have been a kind of naming, and naming was dangerous.

On the last night of February the fog came in off the sea, thick as wool, and the moon rose behind it like a coin under milk. In the cave at the headland's foot, Rhys sat with his back to the wet rock and watched the abbey's lights blur across the water. Four months, counted by the falcon's comings and goings and by the ache that had not once left his chest. He had sworn an oath in the mews — if you ever need me, I will find a way — and she had begged him not to, and he had sworn it anyway. But it was not her need that moved him now; it was his own, and he hated it, and it would not be denied.

He knew the abbey's secret ways. Old Tom had shown him as a boy: the monks' stair behind the chapel's fallen wall, the tunnel from the wine cellars up into the west tower, where the floor had rotted and no one went. Tom called them the abbey's veins — a man who knew them could walk through the heart of the house and never be seen. Rhys had never needed them. He needed them now.

He came up through the dark like a fish through water, moving by touch, breath shallow, feet placed like a man crossing a frozen stream. He had meant only to see her: to stand in the gallery's shadow and watch the shape of her through a crack in a door, and carry that away into whatever years were left. But when he reached the landing above her rooms and heard, through the old timber, the small sound of her breathing, awake, sleepless in the vast cold bed, the plan fell away from him like a coat he no longer needed.

The door gave on oiled hinges. She was sitting up in the dark, her hand at her throat, moonlight through the fog laid pale across her face. She did not scream. She looked at him one long, terrible moment, the way one looks at a ghost, not believing, then believing, then grieving, and then she was out of the bed and in his arms, with no sound in the world but their breath and the sea grinding below.

"You'll be killed," she whispered against his neck. "You'll be killed, and it will be my doing."

"Hush. I had to see you. Once more. I'd have gone mad."

They had only moments, and both knew it. He pressed something into her hand, a falcon's feather, gray and barred, and she closed her fingers over it like a holy thing. "Go," she said. "Go now, while the fog holds—"

But the fog had not held. Below in the court a voice called out, sharp, a guard's voice, then another, and a lantern flared through the mist like a blade. Marlowe's men, who had never trusted the sea cave or the man in it.

It was not a plan now but a panic, pure and animal. Rhys was down the stair and out through the tunnel mouth onto the headland before the first shout found its name, and the shouts followed him like flung stones: "There! The wall! After him!" and he ran. The mist thinned on the heights; the moon rode clear and white and merciless; the cliff path ran before him like chalk laid down for his death. He knew every step — he had walked it a thousand dawns with her hand in his — and it carried him past the first hundred yards, the second, the gorse-choked hollow where the drop opened to his left, until the lanterns came up behind him, gaining, and stones skipped past his ears.

He did not look back. He could not. The path narrowed, crumbling at the edge where the winter sea had eaten the rock, and the mist closed in again, sudden as a curtain, and he was running blind. He heard Elara's voice then, thin and high from the lit window above the wall, screaming his name, and he turned his head, just once, the way a man turns to see the sun before the dark takes him, and his foot found the edge where the path was no longer a path.

He cried out. The cry went up into the fog and came down again, and Elara heard it from her window, heard it, and knew, with the absolute certainty of the drowned, that he was gone. On the water below, something white turned once in the mist, like a falcon folding its wings, and the sea closed over it, and there was nothing left but the grind of the tide and the shouting of the guards, and the feather in her hand, warm from his body, and gone cold.

She stood at the glass a long time. Behind her, in the great bed, Marlowe slept on, untroubled, a man who had never once dreamed of the cliffs. On the water, where the fog had swallowed the last of the moon, the sea went on grinding, patient as a debt, patient as the years, patient as the heart of the only woman he had ever loved, which did not break, because it had been broken already, and had learned to keep beating.

set.name: Lord Ashworth
set.description: Gaunt, gray-bearded master of Thornfield Abbey, crushed by debts but satisfied the estate is saved. Since the Michaelmas wedding he has grown weary and aged, still blind to the depth of what he broke. He kept his oath on his dead wife's grave: Rhys was spared the frame and the noose, given his life and a little coin and sent from the abbey grounds. He allowed Marlowe to winter at Thornfield. He is unaware of the events of the last night of February—Rhys's secret return, the chase, and the fall—though by morning the household will know a man was driven off the cliffs. He did not act this night; his daughter is Marlowe's concern now, and the estate is saved.

set.name: Rhys
set.description: DEAD. The banished groundskeeper, orphan raised by old Tom, who knew the abbey's secret ways (the monks' stair behind the chapel's fallen wall, the tunnel from the wine cellars up into the west tower—'the abbey's veins,' as Tom called them). Four months after the Michaelmas wedding, unable to bear the distance and bound by his oath (if you ever need me, I will find a way), he slipped back into the estate through the secret passages on the last night of February under cover of fog and a milked moon, meaning only to glimpse Elara. When he heard her awake and sleepless in her rooms he went to her: one brief, stolen, bittersweet embrace; he pressed a falcon's feather into her hand and she begged him to go while the fog held. Marlowe's guards were alerted by a shout and lantern; Rhys fled through the tunnel mouth onto the headland and ran the cliff path in moonlight and mist, the guards gaining, stones skipping past his ears. He heard Elara scream his name from the lit window and turned his head once, lost his footing on the crumbling edge in the mist, cried out, and plunged into the sea below. His body is never found; the sea closed over him and there was nothing left but the tide. His oath is fulfilled in death; he loved Elara beyond all reason to the last.

set.name: Viscount Marlowe
set.description: Wealthy, cold nobleman, married to Elara at Michaelmas, wintering at Thornfield while his southern house is set in order. He is not cruel, simply elsewhere: reading ledgers at dinner, sleeping like a stone, touching her with the absent certainty of a man touching his own furniture. On the last night of February his guards (who never trusted the sea cave or the man in it) were alerted during Rhys's secret visit and gave chase across the moonlit cliffs; Rhys fell from the crumbling edge into the sea. Marlowe slept untroubled through the cry, a man who has never once dreamed of the cliffs, unaware of the bond that died that night or of his wife standing at the glass with a falcon's feather in her hand.

set.name: The Falcon
set.description: Young female falcon rescued from a snare, healed in the mews, flying free over the cliffs; the living bond between Elara and Rhys, invoked in oaths in the cave and the mews. After the Michaelmas wedding she turned once, twice, over the water and was gone into the light; in a hard white January noon Elara saw her again, a dark arrow against the snow-light, turning once over the water, gone. On the night of Rhys's death, as he plunged into the sea, something white turned once in the mist on the water below, like a falcon folding its wings, and the sea closed over it. Still free, still occasionally seen over the cliffs—in the years to come Elara will whisper Rhys's name to the wounded falcons that come to her.

set.name: Lady Elara Ashworth (now Lady Marlowe)
set.description: Nineteen, widow in name only—still married to Viscount Marlowe, who survives her. Since the Michaelmas wedding she has lived through a winter at Thornfield as the hollow, obedient Lady Marlowe: rising with the house, smiling at the county, saying 'my lord' in the right places; Marlowe is not cruel but absent, reading ledgers, sleeping like a stone. She survives by inches and has learned survival is its own slow wound. She never stopped thinking of Rhys; from her window (her father's old rooms) she watches the headland and the storm cave, and saw the falcon once in a hard January noon, which she told herself meant nothing. She never asked about Rhys, knowing naming is dangerous; she does not know where he is, though the servants whisper of a wild man living in the sea cave who watches the abbey like a dog at a shut door. On the last night of February, in fog and a milked moon, Rhys came to her through the secret ways; she woke to find him at her bedside, gave no scream, and held him in one single stolen embrace; he pressed a falcon's feather into her hand. Marlowe's guards were alerted; Rhys fled along the moonlit cliffs; from her window she heard his cry as he lost his footing in the mist on the crumbling edge and plunged into the sea below, and she knows with absolute certainty he is gone. She stood at the glass a long time while Marlowe slept untroubled, the feather in her hand warm from his body and then gone cold; her heart did not break because it had been broken already and learned to keep beating. Desperately in love, hollowed, grief-struck, certain of Rhys's death, still married to Marlowe who winters at Thornfield.

On the last night of February, in thick sea fog and a milked moon, banished Rhys slipped back into Thornfield through the abbey's secret ways taught him by old Tom (the monks' stair behind the chapel's fallen wall, the tunnel from the wine cellars up into the west tower), meaning only to glimpse Elara but going to her bedside when he heard her awake; she woke, did not scream, and they shared one brief stolen embrace in the shadows of her chambers, where he pressed a falcon's feather into her hand.

Marlowe's guards, who had never trusted the sea cave or the man in it, were alerted by a shout and a lantern flaring through the fog; Rhys fled through the tunnel mouth onto the headland and ran the cliff path in moonlight and closing mist, the guards gaining and stones skipping past his ears; hearing Elara scream his name from the lit window he turned his head once, lost his footing on the crumbling edge, cried out, and plunged into the sea below.

Rhys's body is never found; the sea closed over him in the mist and there was nothing left but the grind of the tide and the shouting of the guards. Elara heard his cry from her window and knew with absolute certainty that he was gone; she stood at the glass a long time while Marlowe slept untroubled, the falcon's feather in her hand growing cold. The wild man the servants whispered lived in the sea cave is gone; his oath that if Elara ever needed him he would find a way to her is fulfilled in death.

Elara keeps the falcon's feather Rhys pressed into her hand on the night of his death; it becomes her only relic of him, carried through the years into widowhood and her return to Thornfield (Chapter 9).

In the years after Rhys's death Elara will return to Thornfield as a widow and tend the wounded falcons that come to the cliffs, whispering to them the name of Rhys, the man she loved beyond all reason (Chapter 9).

chapters.name: The Ghost of Thornfield
chapters.content:
Years passed, and the sea kept no ledger. It took the seasons in turn and gave back nothing but the tide, patient as a debt, and Elara lived the only way a woman learns to live after the heart has been spent: she went on.

The viscount's death was a quiet thing, an autumn fever that carried him off in his own southern house while Elara sat at his bedside because it was her place, and felt nothing at all, not grief, not gladness, not even relief. He was not cruel; he had only been elsewhere, and now he was elsewhere forever. The lawyers wrote her name in documents, and the title passed to a cousin she had never met, and the widow's portion was a modest thing, and she took it, and she came home.

Thornfield Abbey had not waited for her. The roof had let in the weather in a dozen places; the ivy had taken the east tower as a man takes a fortress. Her father was dead these four years, buried beside her mother on the cliff, and the estate, mortgaged to the last window sash, had been sold to a London man who had no use for the northern wind. But the old steward had remembered her, and the London man was kind in his absent way, and so a plain room in the west wing was aired, and a fire lit, and the servants of the great house—a wild woman, they whispered, a widow, mad or near it—laid a place for her at the table she did not come to.

She went to the cliffs instead. It was spring when she came home, and the gorse was gold, and the air off the sea had the taste she had carried in her mouth for years like a coin kept under the tongue. She walked the long crumble of the path she had climbed with Rhys's hand in hers, a lifetime and no time at all ago, and the wind took her hair—silvered now, gone gray at the temples, then white as gull-wing—and she did not search the horizon. She had stopped searching the horizon years ago. She only looked, because the looking was what was left.

The villagers told each other stories about her. She was a ghost, they said, a woman who belonged neither to the living nor to the dead, and some of them half believed it. She would stand on the headland for hours in weather that would strip the skin off a man, her white hair blown about her face, her eyes fixed on nothing, and the children who saw her from the lower fields would cross themselves and run. The fishermen learned to row wide of the point, because once, at dusk, they swore they saw her raise her hand to the water as though beckoning, or blessing, or waving to someone only she could see.

She did not correct them. There was no correcting to be done. They were right, in their way: she had died on the last night of February, in a year the sea had since washed from its memory, and whatever walked the cliffs now was the shape that was left.

In the mews, where the roof had fallen and the birds of prey had come and gone for decades, she built what comfort she could. She was not Rhys; she had none of his sure hands or his land-lore, only the scraps of it he had taught her on the stolen dawns—woundwort, yarrow, comfrey, how to bind a wing with a splint of hazel, how to read a bird's fear in its eye. Wounded falcons came to the cliffs, as they always had, blown inland by storms or struck down by the sea wind, and she took them in. The servants learned to leave scraps of meat at the mews door, and the falconer's rough gloves she had found in a chest, and to keep away.

To each bird that mended she told the same thing. She held it hooded and quiet on her wrist and whispered to it the name of a man she had loved beyond all reason—Rhys, she said, Rhys—and the falcons, who knew nothing of grief, turned their heads at the sound and watched her with their flat, fierce, ancient eyes, and flew free when their wings were ready, and sometimes returned, as Rhys had once said such birds do, to the place where the kindness was.

And on a hard white noon in the first winter of her return, as she stood on the headland with the salt crusting her lips and the wind tearing at her shawl, she saw the falcon. She would have known her anywhere: the young female of the snare, of the mews, of the dawn lessons and the first kiss. The bird turned once, twice, over the water, dark as an arrow against the snow-light, and Elara raised her hand to it as the fishermen swore she did, and did not know if she was blessing it or beseeching it.

The falcon turned a third time. Something in the old, wild breast of the woman on the cliff cracked, and out of it, unbidden, came the cry that had been locked in her for nine years and a winter—his name, flung at the sky the way he had flung his on the night of his fall, into fog that swallowed it whole.

The falcon banked, and was gone into the light.

Elara stood on the wind-scoured rocks a long time, alone, and below her the sea went on grinding, patient as a debt, patient as the years, patient as grief. The waves rose and fell against the cliff in the same rhythm they had kept before she was born and would keep after she was nothing but wind. They did not know his name. They did not know hers. They only remembered the shape of a love that was never allowed to live, and broke against the stone with it, again and again, forever, which is the only way the sea knows how to mourn.

set.name: Lady Elara Ashworth
set.description: Same woman as Lady Marlowe the widow; the young lord's daughter is now a silver-haired widow of about twenty-eight, back at Thornfield Abbey where she was born. Father dead these four years, viscount dead of autumn fever, estate sold to a London man who gave her a plain west-wing room. Known to villagers as a ghost; walks the cliffs and tends wounded falcons, whispering Rhys's name to each; keeps his falcon feather; saw the falcon once more in a hard white noon, turned three times and gone, and cried his name into the sky. Alone at the story's end on the wind-scoured rocks, the tide grinding below.

set.name: Lord Ashworth
set.description: DEAD. The gaunt, gray-bearded master of Thornfield Abbey died four years before Elara's return and is buried beside his wife on the cliff. He never knew Rhys's fate on the last night of February. The estate he saved with his daughter's marriage was mortgaged to the last window sash and was sold to a London man with no use for the northern wind. He was spared ever understanding the full depth of what he broke.

set.name: Rhys
set.description: DEAD. The banished groundskeeper, orphan raised by old Tom, who knew the abbey's secret ways (the monks' stair behind the chapel's fallen wall, the tunnel from the wine cellars up into the west tower—'the abbey's veins'). He slipped back to Thornfield on the last night of February through the secret passages, shared one brief stolen embrace with Elara and pressed a falcon's feather into her hand, fled Marlowe's guards along the moonlit cliffs, and plunged from the crumbling edge into the sea; his body is never found. The sea closed over him; there was nothing left but the tide. His oath is fulfilled in death; he loved Elara beyond all reason to the last. In the years after, Elara returns to Thornfield as a widow and whispers his name to the wounded falcons on the cliffs, so his memory endures in the place where the kindness was.

set.name: Viscount Marlowe
set.description: DEAD. The wealthy, cold nobleman who married Elara at Michaelmas died of an autumn fever in his own southern house (the autumn of some later year), with Elara at his bedside doing her duty and feeling nothing—not grief, not gladness, not relief. He was never cruel, only elsewhere; the title passed to a cousin she never met, and she was left a modest widow's portion. To the last he never once dreamed of the cliffs, unaware of the bond that died on the last night of February or of the woman standing at the glass with a falcon's feather in her hand.

set.name: The Falcon
set.description: The young female falcon rescued from the snare and healed in the mews—the living bond between Elara and Rhys. She appeared to Elara on a hard white January noon after the wedding, and on the night of Rhys's death something white turned once in the mist on the water, like a falcon folding its wings. Years later, in the first winter of Elara's return to Thornfield, she came again: a dark arrow against the snow-light, turning once, twice, three times over the water as Elara raised her hand and cried out Rhys's name, then banked and was gone into the light. As Rhys once said, such birds return to the place where the kindness was; she still comes to the cliffs, where Elara tends the wounded falcons that follow her.

set.name: Lady Elara Ashworth (now Lady Marlowe)
set.description: Twenty-eight, widow in name and in spirit. The Viscount Marlowe died of an autumn fever in his southern house; the title passed to a cousin and she was left a modest widow's portion. She returned to Thornfield Abbey in spring, a few years after her father's death (Lord Ashworth died four years before her return, buried beside his wife on the cliff; the mortgaged estate had been sold to a London man who gave her a plain room in the west wing). Her hair is silvered, gone white as gull-wing; the villagers call her a ghost, a woman who belongs neither to the living nor to the dead. She walks the same cliffs where she and Rhys once dreamed, no longer searching the horizon, only looking. She tends the wounded falcons that come to the cliffs in the fallen mews, using the scraps of Rhys's land-lore (woundwort, yarrow, comfrey, binding a wing with hazel), whispering to each bird the name of the man she loved beyond all reason—Rhys. She keeps the falcon's feather he pressed into her hand on the night of his death, her only relic of him. On a hard white noon in the first winter of her return she saw the original falcon of the snare turn once, twice, three times over the water and vanish into the light, and she cried out Rhys's name at the sky. The story ends with her alone on the wind-scoured rocks, the waves below echoing the memory of a love that was never allowed to live.

Lord Ashworth died four years before Elara's return to Thornfield and was buried beside his wife on the cliff; the mortgaged estate was sold to a London man who had no use for the northern wind, and the roof and ivy began taking the abbey back.

The Viscount Marlowe died of an autumn fever in his southern house with Elara at his bedside; she felt nothing—not grief, not gladness, not relief. The title passed to a cousin she never met, and she received a modest widow's portion.

Elara returned to Thornfield Abbey as a widow in spring, given a plain room in the west wing by the London owner's kind steward; the villagers called her a ghost, a woman who belonged neither to the living nor the dead, and the fishermen rowed wide of the point where they swore they saw her raise her hand to the water.

In the fallen mews Elara tended the wounded falcons that came to the cliffs, using the scraps of Rhys's land-lore he taught her on the stolen dawns, and whispered to each bird the name of a man she loved beyond all reason—Rhys—before letting them fly free when their wings were ready.

In the first winter of her return to Thornfield, on a hard white noon, Elara saw the falcon of the snare turn once, twice, three times over the water while she raised her hand and cried Rhys's name into the sky; the falcon banked and was gone into the light.
